sections.description: This section lays out the patient’s timeline, initial symptoms, vital findings, and the broad diagnostic possibilities considered when a septic patient presents with pancytopenia, coagulopathy and multi‑organ dysfunction.
subtopics: Dog‑bite exposure and delayed antibiotic use
Early sepsis signs: fever, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, mottled extremities
Laboratory profile on admission: pancytopenia, acute kidney injury, elevated transaminases, coagulopathy
Initial working diagnosis of DIC secondary to bacterial sepsis
Exclusion of surgical emergencies (necrotising fasciitis) by imaging
Early microbiology: aggressive empiric coverage with piperacillin‑tazobactam and suspicion of Capnocytophaga

sections.section_title: 2. Progression to Thrombotic Microangiopathy – Diagnostic Reasoning
sections.description: This section follows the shift from sepsis‑related multi‑organ failure to a distinct microangiopathic process, detailing laboratory evolution, imaging, and the application of scoring systems to rule in or out TTP and other TMAs.
subtopics: Evolution of renal function: anuria, AKI, initiation of CRRT
Emergence of skin bleeding and cyanosis indicating microthrombi
Core laboratory findings of MAHA: drop in hemoglobin, reticulocyte response, schistocyte count, undetectable haptoglobin, rising LDH
Interpretation of DAT and repeat testing
Use of PLASMIC score to assess TTP probability
ADAMTS13 activity result (43.5%) and its exclusion of TTP
Stool PCR to rule out STEC‑HUS
Kidney biopsy findings: acute tubular necrosis, fibrin thrombi, crescents

sections.description: This section explains how Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection can precipitate complement dysregulation in susceptible hosts, outlining genetic versus acquired triggers and the interplay between bacterial capsules and serum complement.
subtopics: Overview of the alternative complement pathway and regulatory proteins (CFH, CFI, CFB, CD46)
Mechanisms of capnestic bacterial complement activation and inhibition
Role of bacterial capsule in complement evasion and host endothelial activation
Genetic predisposition in a subset of CM‑HUS patients and importance of genetic testing
Evidence of infection‑induced CM‑HUS from literature (including recent C. canimorsus cases)
Diagnostic caveats: normal C3/C4 in active disease, complement functional assays

sections.section_title: 4. Therapeutic Strategy – Balancing Infection Control and Complement Blockade
sections.description: This section outlines the step‑wise management decisions, including empiric antibiotic adjustments, supportive care, plasma exchange decisions, and the timing and safety considerations of eculizumab initiation during an active infection.
subtopics: Antibiotic de‑escalation guided by culture results
Use of plasma exchange as bridging therapy; impact on hemolysis and renal recovery
Criteria for initiating eculizumab: persistence of TMA, platelets ≤ 50×10⁹/L, unresolved hemolysis
Vaccination schedule (Menveo, Bexsero) prior to complement inhibition
Prophylactic antibiotics during eculizumab therapy
Monitoring for infectious complications and managing therapeutic windows
Maintenance therapy duration and criteria for discontinuation

sections.description: This section summarizes the patient’s recovery trajectory, laboratory remission, renal function outcomes, and highlights key lessons for clinicians regarding early recognition, diagnosis, and management of CM‑HUS triggered by uncommon bacterial infections.
subtopics: Timeline of hemolysis resolution and renal recovery after eculizumab
Ongoing renal function: serum creatinine, estimated GFR, dialysis independence
Extended complement and genetic testing results, interpretation of negative findings
Prognostic factors: time to eculizumab initiation, initial renal status, TMA severity
Clinical take‑aways: high index of suspicion for TMA in septic patients with persistent thrombocytopenia and hemolysis
Importance of rapid molecular diagnostics (e.g., real‑time nanopore sequencing) for fastidious organisms
Avoidance of unnecessary invasive procedures (bone marrow biopsy) when clinical picture favors sepsis
Future directions: data registries for infection‑triggered CM‑HUS, research into complement‐inhibitor safety profiles
